PSYCHIATRIC ADVANCE DIRECTIVE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Taylor Morgan

MENTAL HEALTH TREATMENT PREFERENCES DECLARATION
I, Jordan Alex Lee, being an adult of sound mind, state these instructions regarding my mental health treatment, for use during any future period when I have been determined to lack the capacity to make my own mental health treatment decisions. Regarding medications I prefer or wish to refuse for treatment of a mental health condition: ☐ approve: sertraline; refuse: lithium. Regarding hospitalization or inpatient treatment: ☐ prefer voluntary admission over involuntary hold where possible. Regarding my preferred mental health treatment facility or providers: ☐ Acme Behavioral Health Center. Regarding electroconvulsive therapy (ECT): ☐ generally opposed to ECT except as a last resort. I designate Taylor Morgan as the person I want consulted about these instructions and, if Taylor Morgan is unable, unwilling, or not reasonably available, Riley Chen. Additional instructions regarding my mental health care: ☐ None.

NO SEPARATE MENTAL HEALTH ADVANCE DIRECTIVE STATUTE
California does not maintain a separate statute for a "mental health advance directive." A statement of Jordan Alex Lee's wishes for future mental health treatment is created and governed the same way as any other advance health care directive, under the single Health Care Decisions Law (Cal. Prob. Code § 4600 et seq.), because that law's own definition of "health care" already covers a patient's mental health condition, not just physical health.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This division may be cited as the Health Care Decisions Law."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4600 (California Legislative Information text), the short title of the single, general statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4600.)
  "“Health care” means any care, treatment, service, or procedure to maintain, diagnose, or otherwise affect a patient’s physical or mental health condition."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4615 (California Legislative Information text), the statute's definition of "health care," covering mental as well as physical health (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4615.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that California addresses mental health treatment wishes within its one general Health Care Decisions Law rather than through a separate, dedicated "mental health advance directive" statute — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. Both citations below sit in the same division and part of the Probate Code (Division 4.7, Part 1, Chapter 1) rather than in unrelated bodies of law, so they are read together as evidence of that single division's own structure and scope, not as two independent confirmations from separate legal sources.

WHAT THIS DIRECTIVE MAY ADDRESS
Within the same Health Care Decisions Law that governs any advance health care directive, a statement of Jordan Alex Lee's wishes for future mental health treatment may address the selection or discharge of specific mental health care providers and treatment facilities, and the approval or disapproval of specific mental health medications or programs of medication. California's own optional statutory advance directive form reflects this same scope, describing an agent's authority in matching terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(a) “Health care decision” means a decision made by a patient or the patient’s agent, conservator, or surrogate, regarding the patient’s health care, including the following: (1) Selection and discharge of health care providers and institutions. (2) Approval or disapproval of diagnostic tests, surgical procedures, and programs of medication, including mental health conditions."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4617(a) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory definition of what counts as a "health care decision," including medication programs for mental health conditions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4617.)
  "(b) Select or discharge health care providers and institutions. (c) For all physical and mental health care, approve or disapprove diagnostic tests, surgical procedures, and programs of medication."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4701 (California Legislative Information text, statutory advance health care directive form), the statutory form's matching description of provider selection and medication approval/disapproval for mental health care (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4701.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of the actual categories of mental-health-specific content the law recognizes — not a generic, assumed list, and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. The second citation is drawn from the explanatory and operative text of California's own statutory advance directive form (§ 4701), which corroborates § 4617's definition in plain language but is still part of the same Health Care Decisions Law rather than an independent body of law.

WHAT THIS DIRECTIVE CANNOT AUTHORIZE: COMMITMENT AND ECT
Regardless of what Jordan Alex Lee writes in a mental health treatment directive, and regardless of what authority is given to Taylor Morgan, the Health Care Decisions Law itself does not authorize anyone to consent, on Jordan Alex Lee's behalf, to commitment to or placement in a mental health treatment facility, or to convulsive treatment — a defined term that includes electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). California's own optional statutory advance directive form states the same limitation directly to the person filling it out.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "This division does not authorize consent to any of the following on behalf of a patient: (a) Commitment to or placement in a mental health treatment facility. (b) Convulsive treatment (as defined in Section 5325 of the Welfare and Institutions Code)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4652 (California Legislative Information text), the statutory bar on consenting to mental health facility commitment or convulsive treatment under this division (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4652.)
  "However, your agent will not be able to commit you to a mental health facility, or consent to convulsive treatment, psychosurgery, sterilization, or abortion for you."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4701 (California Legislative Information text, statutory advance health care directive form), the statutory form's own plain-language statement of the same limitation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4701.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence of a real, categorical statutory carve-out from what any advance health care directive can authorize under this division — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. The second citation corroborates the first in plain language but is drawn from the same Health Care Decisions Law (the statutory form itself, § 4701) rather than an independent body of law.

ELECTROCONVULSIVE THERAPY HAS ITS OWN SEPARATE CONSENT PROCEDURE
Consent to convulsive treatment, including electroconvulsive therapy, is governed by a separate statutory scheme in the Welfare and Institutions Code (part of the Lanterman-Petris-Short Act), not by the Health Care Decisions Law that governs the rest of this directive. That scheme gives a person a statutory right to refuse convulsive treatment, and — where written informed consent to it is given at all — requires that consent to be time-limited (to no more than 30 days of treatment) and freely revocable at any time.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "(f) To refuse convulsive treatment including, but not limited to, any electroconvulsive treatment, any treatment of the mental condition which depends on the induction of a convulsion by any means, and insulin coma treatment."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 5325(f) (California Legislative Information text), the statutory right to refuse convulsive treatment, defined to include electroconvulsive treatment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=5325.)
  "The patient gives written informed consent as defined in Section 5326.5 to the convulsive treatment. Such consent shall be for a specified maximum number of treatments over a specified maximum period of time not to exceed 30 days, and shall be revocable at any time before or between treatments."
  — Cal. Welf. & Inst. Code § 5326.7(d) (California Legislative Information text), the time-limited, revocable nature of written informed consent to convulsive treatment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=WIC&sectionNum=5326.7.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statutes, used as real evidence that California regulates convulsive treatment consent through a distinct statutory scheme with its own time-limited, revocable consent requirement — not a full account of every procedural safeguard in that scheme (which also includes, for patients who cannot give that contemporaneous consent, review by a two-physician committee and, if capacity is disputed, a superior court hearing), and not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a genuinely complex, only partially verified area: this session did not verify whether, or how, a written mental-health treatment directive's ECT-related wishes are actually taken into account within that separate Welfare and Institutions Code procedure — the two statutory schemes were confirmed to be independent, but their practical interaction was not verified and is not asserted here. The two citations below are from two different, independently numbered sections of the Welfare and Institutions Code, not subsections of one section.

CAPACITY DETERMINATION USES THE SAME RULE AS THE GENERAL DIRECTIVE
The Health Care Decisions Law does not set a different or additional capacity-determination rule for the mental-health-treatment portion of an advance directive. The same default rule that applies to the rest of an advance health care directive applies here: unless this directive specifies otherwise, a determination that Jordan Alex Lee lacks or has recovered the capacity needed for these mental health treatment instructions (or for Taylor Morgan's authority regarding them) to take or lose effect is made by Jordan Alex Lee's primary physician.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Unless otherwise specified in a written advance health care directive, for the purposes of this division, a determination that a patient lacks or has recovered capacity, or that another condition exists that affects an individual health care instruction or the authority of an agent or surrogate, shall be made by the primary physician."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4658 (California Legislative Information text), the single, general capacity-determination default rule, with no mental-health-specific variant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4658.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that no separate mental-health-specific capacity rule exists — the same general rule already used in this site's Advance Health Care Directive document applies, and is cited again here only so this document is independently complete on its own. This is a single statutory section (§ 4658); no additional independent source was found for this, and none was needed since the point is that no distinct rule exists.

THIS DIRECTIVE CAN BE LIMITED TO TAKE EFFECT ONLY IN SPECIFIED CIRCUMSTANCES
Jordan Alex Lee's written mental health treatment instructions do not have to take effect immediately or unconditionally. Under the same Health Care Decisions Law, an individual health care instruction may be limited so that it only takes effect if a specified condition arises — for example, only during a future period when Jordan Alex Lee has been determined to lack the capacity to make mental health treatment decisions.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "An adult having capacity may give an individual health care instruction. The individual instruction may be oral or written. The individual instruction may be limited to take effect only if a specified condition arises."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 4670 (California Legislative Information text), authority for an individual health care instruction to be conditional (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=4670.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as real evidence that a written instruction can be made conditional on a stated future circumstance — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific directive. This is a single statutory section (§ 4670); no additional independent source was found for this.

SIGNATURES AND WITNESSES
Signature of Jordan Alex Lee: ☐ _________________________ Date: ☐ _________________________

This directive is signed either before a notary public or in the presence of two qualified witnesses, whose acknowledgment or signatures and declarations appear on an attached page.
